data.text: A model of natural walking behavior can be used for system-controlled VR navigation to provide a realistic walking experience. The development of this model is carried out in four steps: empirical research, data analysis, model creation, and validation.
points: A natural walking behavior model provides a realistic walking experience for system-controlled VR navigation.
Developing this model involves four steps: empirical research, data analysis, model creation, and validation.

data.text: An empirical study with 40 participants of various ages and heights was conducted to collect real-life walking data for a speed estimation model. The study used a physical corridor with seven paintings at specific distances to simulate points of interest in a virtual tour. Participants stopped at each painting to take a photo while a smartphone camera recorded their foot movements.
points: An empirical study with 40 participants of various ages and heights was conducted to collect real-life walking data for a speed estimation model.
The study used a physical corridor with seven paintings at specific distances to simulate points of interest in a virtual tour.
Participants stopped at each painting to take a photo while a smartphone camera recorded their foot movements.

data.text: Step frequency was computed by manually playing videos and noting foot-strike timestamps and distances. This revealed a "slow-in-slow-out" pattern where step frequency starts low, peaks, plateaus, and then decreases to zero at the target. Velocity slows just before the target because users know they must stop to take a photo.
points: Step frequency was computed by manually playing videos and noting foot-strike timestamps and distances.
A "slow-in-slow-out" pattern was observed where step frequency starts low, peaks, plateaus, and then decreases to zero at the target.
Velocity slows just before the target because users know they must stop to take a photo.

data.text: The slow-in-slow-out walking pattern is modeled using a Fourier-series expansion of harmonically related sinusoids based on empirical data. Because users typically perceive visual flow more slowly than actual movement, the perceived scene-change speed must differ from the actual speed to ensure natural behavior. This is achieved by multiplying the actual walking speed by a visual gain g, which is typically set to 2.10.
points: The slow-in-slow-out walking pattern is modeled using a Fourier-series expansion of harmonically related sinusoids based on empirical data.
A Fourier series can approximate any continuous periodic function with arbitrary precision using its first few terms.
To create natural walking behavior, the perceived scene-change speed must differ from the actual movement speed.
Perceived speed is computed by multiplying the actual walking speed by a visual gain g, which is typically set to 2.10.

data.text: The natural walking speed model is formed by multiplying computed natural walking behavior by a visual gain factor. An empirical study comparing instantaneous speed to constant average speed showed that instantaneous speed significantly improved realism and user preference. While the model is suitable for realistic walking and likely to increase presence, it does not alone address cybersickness and requires additional measures.
points: The natural walking speed model is formed by multiplying computed natural walking behavior by a visual gain factor.
An empirical study compared instantaneous natural walking speed with constant average speed.
Instantaneous speed produced significantly higher realism ratings and user preference.
The model is suitable for realistic walking experiences and likely to increase presence.
This model alone does not address cybersickness and requires additional measures.
